A 55-year-old woman with a history of IDDM, hyper-
tension, hypothyroidism, and gastroesophageal reﬂux dis-
ease presented with a 4-week course of lower back muscle
spasms, diplopia, and gait difﬁculties. On examination she
had downbeating nystagmus of moderate amplitude and
frequency in primary gaze. An alternating inferior rectus
skew deviation was evident with a right hypertropia in
right lateral gaze and a left hypertropia in left lateral gaze.
She also had minimally increased tone in all extremities
and signiﬁcant dysmetria and appendicular ataxia on the
left. Cerbrospinal ﬂuid examination showed a white blood
cell count of 6 cells/ml and a minimally elevated protein
value of 61 mg/dl. Studies for known paraneoplastic
antibodies (including Anti-Yo, Hu, Ma1, Ma2, Ri, CV2/
CRMP5) were negative. GAD antibodies were detected in
both the serum and CSF using immunohistochemistry and
radioimmunoanalysis (Figure 1). Brain magnetic resonance
imaging was normal with no Arnold-Chiari malformation
observed. Brain ﬂuoro-deoxyglucose positron emission to-
mography was also unremarkable. Computed tomography
scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal.
The patient was treated with diazepam and intravenous
methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days), which resulted in
improvement in her muscle spasm but no change in her
other symptoms. Subsequently, she received intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIg, 0.4 gm/kg/day) for 5 days, and a

signiﬁcant reduction in nystagmus, and a reduction in
dysmetria were noted.
The neuro-opthalmic ﬁndings in our patient are most
likely due to cerebellar dysfunction and the effect of GAD
antibodies on GABAergic transmission.
4 Lesions within the
posterior midline of the cerebellum may produce downbeat-
ing nystagmus.
5 We know of no other studies that fully
describe the neuro-opthalmic consequences of GAD antibod-
ies. As demonstrated by this case, patients with GAD
antibodies may have elements of both Stiff-person syndrome
(muscle rigidity and spasms) and prominent cerebellar dys-
function. Treatment with diazepam may rapidly improve Stiff-
person symptoms, whereas IVIg may allow for improvement in
cerebellar dysfunction, including downbeat nystagmus.
